How to Focus During Prayer: What to Do When Your Mind Wanders

Everyone gets distracted during prayer, even the saints. Don’t scold yourself; calmly come back with a short “Lord, help me,” familiar words of Scripture and fewer words of your own. The stories of Teresa of Ávila, Edward Pusey, Abbess Arsenia and Brother Lawrence.

By Lampada team · Published 2026-10-20

Ávila, the Convent of the Incarnation. A nun spends the hour of prayer she has set herself waiting, not for God, but for the clock to strike. Years later she will admit: “Very often, and for some years, I cared more about wishing the hour I had set myself would be over, and about listening for the clock to strike, than about other good things”1. And: “Many times, I think, I would have undertaken any severe penance more gladly than settled down to pray”1.

That nun was Teresa of Ávila. She would go on to reform the Carmelite order and write books people still read, and almost four centuries later she would become one of the first women the Catholic Church named a Doctor of the Church2.

If your mind wanders during prayer, you are in good company. Everyone gets distracted, even saints, and it doesn’t mean your prayer has failed. Don’t scold yourself for every distraction: when you notice it, calmly come back to the words of your prayer. A short “Lord, help me,” the familiar words of a psalm or a Gospel passage, and fewer words overall all help. The task that suddenly came to mind can wait. And if you keep nodding off, rest first. Here is how four very different people learned this.

Years with a book in hand

In her Life, Teresa describes her weakness without dressing it up. There were times when she could only walk into the oratory by summoning every bit of courage she had, because a heavy sadness came over her there, and it was the Lord who helped her get past it3. And she noticed something: “After I had forced myself like this, I found more quiet and delight than at some times when I wanted to pray”1.

She believed the Lord had deliberately left her without a teacher. For eighteen years, years of great dryness when she could not meditate in prayer, she never dared to begin praying without a book, except right after Communion3: “my soul was as afraid to be at prayer without it as if it were going out to fight a whole crowd”1. The book “was like a companion or a shield”1, taking the blows her many thoughts rained down on her3. Many times she simply opened the book3. “Nothing more was needed: sometimes I read a little, sometimes a lot, according to the grace the Lord gave me”1.

For Teresa, distraction was not a verdict on her prayer but a difficulty she lived with for years. And leaning on someone else’s words was no disgrace to her; it was a lifeline.

The same hour and the same weakness appear in the Gospel. In the garden of Gethsemane, Jesus comes back to His disciples and finds them asleep. “Were you not able to keep watch with Me for one hour?” He asks Peter. And then: “Watch and pray so that you will not enter into temptation. For the spirit is willing, but the body is weak” (Matthew 26:40–41)4. He sees their weakness and still calls them to keep watch and pray.

“God help me!”

For more than fifty years Edward Pusey was Professor of Hebrew at Oxford, and he was one of the leaders of the Oxford Movement in the Church of England5. Yet the voice in his Spiritual Letters is not a scholar’s but a confessor’s. In 1847 a woman he guided wrote to him that her mind kept wandering when she prayed. Pusey’s first guess was the simplest one: “I hope the distractions you speak of were rather the effect of sleepiness”6. Then he urged her to take a proper rest before Lent arrived6.

In another letter from 1847, Pusey explains what to do at the very moment you realize your thoughts have drifted. Rather than resolving to concentrate harder or stopping to repent of the lapse, send up one instant, simple cry for help, “God help me!”, and plunge straight back into the words you were praying, since a two-part response is a distraction in itself6. He adds: “Involuntary distraction is infirmity, not sin.”6

The rest of his advice is just as down to earth. A good thought that turns up at the wrong moment can be asked to wait its turn, or entrusted to your guardian angel to keep for you6. And when the children are pressing you to hurry, make them the subject of your prayer6. “Be not anxious about many prayers, but about praying much.”6

His “God help me!” sits well beside a line from the psalms: “Give me an undivided heart, that I may fear Your name” (Psalm 86:11)7. It is a prayer for anyone whose heart is pulled in ten directions at once.

You don’t need a dark cell

Anna Sebryakova, the daughter of a landowner from the Don Cossack lands, entered the Ust-Medveditsa convent on the Don at seventeen and was its abbess for more than forty years. In 2016 the Orthodox Church canonized Abbess Arsenia as a locally venerated saint8. In 1871, writing to Pyotr Brianchaninov, the brother of St Ignatius Brianchaninov9, she makes an admission you would hardly expect from an abbess: “I avoid talking about prayer, because I do not have it myself”10.

Here is what she did herself, turning to canons, extended hymns used in Orthodox prayer: “Sometimes, when I am badly distracted and inattentive, I turn my attention to reading the canons to the Mother of God and to the saints, but in order to direct my attention toward prayer, not to turn it away from prayer to reading”10. Nor does she hide what props her up: “we need dark cells for recollection, like mine in the garden, which I call my ‘infirmity’”10. “But all these are temporary aids; nothing helps me as much as life itself”10. And that summer she laments: “somehow I have become very scattered and caught up in the bustle”10.

Props help, but you don’t have to wait for perfect quiet: even an abbess with a dark cell in her garden lived a busy, scattered life.

Her correspondent’s brother, St Ignatius Brianchaninov, a Russian bishop, gives a general rule in his letter “On Attention in Prayer”: “to enclose the mind in the words of the prayer”11. He advises beginners to pray “a little at a time, but often”11. And: “When you are alone, pray aloud enough to hear yourself: this helps you pay attention”11. “If you do not have proper attention in prayer, do not be troubled by it”11: God will give attention in His own time to the one who keeps at prayer and keeps pushing himself to pay attention12.

Brother Lawrence’s kitchen

Nicolas Herman grew up in Lorraine during the Thirty Years’ War, became a soldier out of poverty and was left lame for life by a wound13. Later he was in service as a footman to a treasurer named Fieubert, and by his own account he was so clumsy that nothing was safe in his hands14. At a monastery of the Discalced Carmelites in Paris he became Brother Lawrence and worked for many years as a cook. Abbé Joseph de Beaufort wrote down their conversations, and after Lawrence died they were published with his letters as The Practice of the Presence of God13.

He planned his tasks before he began, deciding what had to be done and in what order, and as he got to work he would ask God to help him remain aware of Him throughout15. Afterward he looked back at how it had gone. A job done well meant thanks to God; a job done badly meant asking forgiveness and then, without losing heart, carrying on with God as if nothing had broken the thread15. He said it made no difference to him whether he was kneeling before the Blessed Sacrament or busy in the bustle of the kitchen with several people wanting something from him at once: in both places he was with God and equally at peace15.

Someone once complained to Lawrence in a letter about wandering thoughts. He begins with comfort: his correspondent is far from alone in this struggle16. He advises against piling up words in prayer, since a flood of words is often what sends the mind off course16. He suggests simply standing before God and owning that you need His help, even when you have nothing to say16. When the mind slips away, he says, don’t get upset, because agitation only scatters it further; let your will lead it back calmly16. There is one more approach, and it concerns the rest of your day: the less you let your mind drift away from God in ordinary hours, the easier it is to gather it at prayer, and a habit of turning to Him often makes it simpler to stay focused when you pray, or at least to bring your attention back16.

For Lawrence, attention in prayer is built out of the whole day.

How to try it today

Start small, and pray more often rather than longer. If you keep nodding off, rest first instead of beating yourself up. Give yourself something to lean on, such as a psalm, a chapter of the Gospels or a prayer you know well, and read slowly, aloud if you like; our articles on lectio divina and praying Scripture go into more detail. When you notice your mind has drifted, say “Lord, help me” and go back, without counting how many times it has happened. A task pops into your head? Let it wait: jot it down on paper and return. Someone comes to mind? Pray for them. If words are hard to find, start with what is on your heart right now, in your own words, about one thing. And say less.

What works for you is something you will have to find out. St Ignatius advised praying aloud when you are alone, while Pusey suggested saying the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed silently to yourself, which leaves less room for distraction, with not even your own voice to pull you away6. And don’t judge your prayer by how many times you got distracted.

Keep your intention in view

In Lampada, prayer begins with an intention: in one sentence you write what you want to talk to God about, and that sentence stays on the screen for the whole prayer. When your thoughts wander, you have something to come back to. You can pray for 5, 15 or 30 minutes, 1 hour, or with no timer, and the buttons let you shorten the time to as little as one minute: better short and often. You don’t have to watch the clock the way Teresa did. When the time is up, the app tells you: “Time is up. You can continue.”

Guiding questions about your intention also bring you back to it. You can skip them, and you can answer by typing or by voice: what you say out loud is easier to hold on to. If you allow it, Lampada finds a Scripture passage that fits what you are praying about, something to lean on, like Teresa’s book, and you can listen to it read by a human narrator. Quiet music is optional: for some people it covers background noise, for others it gets in the way. At the end you can write a short takeaway in your own words, and it is saved in your journal. And reminders on the days and at the times you choose help you pray a little at a time, but often.

What Lampada doesn’t do: there is no place to park thoughts for later, so jot that task down on paper or in your notes app. The app doesn’t notice when you get distracted and doesn’t train your attention, it won’t cure sleepiness or fatigue, and it has no ready-made prayers or canons.

And in the same chapter where she remembers listening for the clock, Teresa writes that God is willing to stay even with those who are far from Him, as long as they let Him be with them for at least two hours a day, even when their minds are full of a thousand cares and worldly thoughts, as hers had been3. You don’t have to wait for your thoughts to quiet down. It is enough to come, and to keep coming back.

Frequently asked questions

Why do I get so distracted during prayer?

Because the mind is restless by nature: Brother Lawrence wrote that the mind is a great wanderer16. Sometimes the cause is simpler, and it is tiredness: in one of his letters Edward Pusey hoped that drowsiness was what lay behind the wandering attention a correspondent had described6.

Is it a sin to get distracted during prayer?

Edward Pusey answered: “Involuntary distraction is infirmity, not sin.”6 St Ignatius Brianchaninov advised: “If you do not have proper attention in prayer, do not be troubled by it”11.

What if I fall asleep while praying?

Get some sleep first: Pusey’s advice in that situation was to take a proper rest6. Our own suggestion: pray sitting or standing rather than lying down, and try praying aloud.

Is it okay to pray from a book?

Yes. For eighteen years Teresa of Ávila did not dare to begin praying without a book, except right after Communion3, and Abbess Arsenia turned to reading canons when she was badly distracted17.
